name: Dana Yilmaz

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for your time, Dana. I'm a researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to tech companies, employers, unions or parties. What you tell me is confidential. Could you start by describing a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm a junior at the Castlegate Estates branch on the ring road, which is part of a big national chain. Most of my day is sales progression, which means once a buyer's offer is accepted I chase the solicitors, the mortgage broker and the surveyor until the sale completes. I'm on the phone and email from nine to six, plus a couple of viewings when the senior negotiators are double-booked. I like ticking a sale through to the keys, it's very satisfying.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you find hard, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Keeping twenty-odd sales in my head at once. Last month I missed that a buyer's mortgage offer was about to expire, and Lorraine, my branch manager, had to sort it out. Chains of four or five sales, where one person pulls out and the whole lot falls over, are exhausting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a decent tool and leave it at that. At work we'd probably use it to draft the chasing emails and nothing more. I'd mention it to Omar, my partner, but I wouldn't post about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, that's fine by me. I'd still have my job, and I'd get time to improve at keeping track of sales. We've got over a year's money saved, partly from Omar's overtime last winter, so there's no money stress.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going, and I'd start using the AI draft tool for my chasing emails once Steve, who sits next to me, said it saved him time. I'd build a better spreadsheet for tracking deadlines like mortgage expiry dates. And we'd keep saving towards a bigger place.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. A bit like nothing happened, which is fine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd wait for Steve to say it saves time. Why wait?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because the last thing head office sent us was a new chasing system that crashed every afternoon for a month. Steve's more of a guinea pig than me. When he says a tool works, it usually does.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would anything still worry you in this world?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Just making another mistake like the mortgage one. A sale falling through because I forgot a mortgage date would be awful for the family buying. That's my real worry, and it's about me getting organised.

say: I'd say AI is a **decent tool**, and leave it there.
I'd mention it to my partner **Omar** but not post online.
think: I keep my job and get time to **improve my tracking**.
Over **a year saved** means no money stress.
do: **Use the draft tool** once my colleague Steve says it works.
**Build a spreadsheet** tracking deadlines like mortgage expiry dates.
S0.quote: A sale falling through because I forgot a mortgage date would be awful for the family buying.
fieldNote: Her worry is her own **organisation**, sharpened by a recent mistake.
She waits for a **trusted colleague** to test tools first.
Head office's **crashing system** made her cautious about new tech.

steps.text: Use the AI email drafter for chasing solicitors once proven
Build a deadline tracker for mortgage offer expiry dates
Keep saving with Omar towards a bigger flat

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a big change and people will need help moving, but it's not the end of the world. At work I'd be practical: if the software does the chasing, show me what I do instead. Online I'd maybe share something about retraining schemes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, my job is pretty much everything AI would take first. Chasing, checking, booking, answering customers, that's sales progression. Head office would put in a system that emails solicitors automatically, and they'd need one progressor for three branches instead of one each.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year I'd learn the new system properly, once it's settled in, so I'm the one they keep. I'd ask Lorraine about moving to the negotiator side, doing viewings and valuations, because that's harder to automate. And I'd keep the savings untouched.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nervous, a bit. Like waiting for exam results you know were mixed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If they only kept one progressor for three branches, would it be you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, maybe not. There's a woman at the north branch called Jen who's been doing it ten years and never misses a date. I'd be better off getting out of progression and into negotiating before that decision gets made.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would Omar say?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Omar would say come and work for him, half joking. He's an electrician and he's always behind on his quotes and invoices. But the card says AI does that sort of office work too, so that's not really a plan.

say: I'd say it's a **big change** but not the end of the world.
I'd ask head office **what I do instead** if software chases solicitors.
think: Sales progression is **basically the card**: chasing, checking, booking.
Head office would need **one progressor** for three branches.
do: **Learn the new system** once it settles in.
**Ask Lorraine** about moving to the **negotiator** side.
S1.quote: My job is pretty much everything AI would take first. Chasing, checking, booking, answering customers, that's sales progression.
fieldNote: She sees her role is among the **most exposed** in the agency.
She plans to **jump to negotiating** before cuts are decided.
She rejects her partner's business as an **escape**, since office work is exposed too.

steps.text: Learn head office's new progression system once it's stable
Ask the branch manager to move into viewings and valuations
Leave the year of savings untouched

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is going to hurt a lot of people, and the government needs to have a plan in place now. I'd be careful at work, because head office would be watching. Online I'd mostly read, not post.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think my job is gone by 2028. Sales progression is all thinking work, and so is most of negotiating once AI can talk to buyers. I'd have to go somewhere hands-on, and the robots come in 2031, so that buys me three years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year, I'd go into Omar's electrical business properly, but on the tools, not the paperwork. I'd train as an electrician's mate and learn EV charger installs, which there's loads of demand for. Meanwhile we'd cut back on holidays and eating out, and live mostly on Omar's income.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Unsettled, but not lost. I have Omar and a plan, and that helps a lot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said earlier Omar's business wasn't a plan. What changed?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the slow one I'd still be an agent, so it didn't make sense. Here the agent job's gone fast, and fitting a car charger in someone's garage is hands-on. That's three years of real work, maybe more if people still want a human in their house.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you cut first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The holiday to Turkey to see my grandparents next summer, which would really upset my mum. Then the gym, then takeaways. We'd keep the savings for the bigger shocks.

say: I'd say it will **hurt many people** and needs a plan now.
I'd stay **careful at work** and mostly read online.
think: Sales progression and most negotiating are **gone by 2028**.
Hands-on work buys **three years** until robots arrive around 2031.
do: **Join Omar's business** on the tools, not the paperwork.
**Train in EV charger** installs as an electrician's mate.
**Cut holidays** and eating out, living on Omar's income.
S2.quote: Fitting a car charger in someone's garage is hands-on. That's three years of real work, maybe more if people still want a human in their house.
fieldNote: She **changed her mind** about Omar's business once the timeline changed.
Having a **household plan** keeps her short of alarmed.
Cutting the **trip to Turkey** is the cost that hurts most.

steps.text: Train as an electrician's mate fitting EV chargers with Omar
Cancel next summer's trip to Turkey to visit grandparents
Live mainly on Omar's electrician income for a year

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is time to plan, and businesses and governments should start now. At work I'd suggest Castlegate retrains people rather than just cutting. I'd say it in the staff survey, which is about the only place they ask.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it's the same ending with a better run-up. I'd still lose the agent job, but I'd have time to qualify properly as an electrician. I'd be 32, which is fine for an apprenticeship.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start an evening electrical course next year while still at Castlegate. I'd use AI tools more at work in the meantime, since they'd help with quoting later. We'd save harder and delay the bigger flat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy but busy. I'd feel okay as long as the course was going well.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you want to stay in property in any way?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe on the side. Lots of landlords I know need someone to sort electrical safety certificates. I could combine knowing the agents with being qualified, which is a bit of a niche.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's your biggest doubt about that plan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Whether I'm actually any good with my hands. I've changed a plug and helped my partner Omar on a few Saturdays, that's it. If I'm rubbish at electrics, I'd need another plan fast.

say: I'd say five years means **planning starts now**.
I'd tell Castlegate in the **staff survey** to retrain, not cut.
think: Same ending, but with a **better run-up** to qualify properly.
At **32** I could still start an electrical apprenticeship.
do: **Use AI tools** more at work for quoting skills later.
**Save harder** and delay the bigger flat.
S3.quote: I've changed a plug and helped my partner Omar on a few Saturdays, that's it. If I'm rubbish at electrics, I'd need another plan fast.
fieldNote: She still expects to **lose the agent job** but feels in control.
She sees a **niche** combining landlords and safety certificates.
Her real doubt is her own **practical skill**.

steps.text: Enrol in an evening electrical installation course next year
Use AI tools at work to practise drafting quotes
Put the bigger-flat plan on hold and save harder

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty of time if people start early. At work I'd probably say it once and then get on with my job. I'd still not post much.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think I'd be fine. I'd move from progression to negotiating over the next few years, and later maybe join Omar. Ten years is long enough that I don't need to decide this week.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep working at Castlegate and push to become a negotiator within two years. I'd start using AI tools more, once they're common, because by then everyone would. Around 2030 I'd decide whether to train in electrics.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly calm, with a little worry in the background.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You've said you'd decide around 2030. What would you be watching for?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Whether the big chains start closing branches. If Castlegate Estates, the chain I work for, shuts two of our five local offices, that's my sign to retrain. Until then, I'd keep my head down and get better at the job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you still go ahead with the bigger flat?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably, yes. Omar's been wanting a garage for his van and tools for ages. Ten years is long enough to pay off a good chunk of a mortgage.

say: I'd say ten years is **plenty of time** if people start early.
I'd mention it **once** at work and move on.
think: I'd move from progression to **negotiating** over a few years.
Ten years means **no need to decide** this week.
do: Push to become a **negotiator** within two years.
**Use AI tools** more once everyone else does.
S4.quote: If Castlegate Estates, the chain I work for, shuts two of our five local offices, that's my sign to retrain.
fieldNote: She sets a **clear trigger**: branch closures by the chain.
She plans to **buy the bigger flat** with a garage for Omar.
Her **steady** style shows in waiting until tools are common.

steps.text: Apply for a negotiator role at Castlegate within two years
Buy a bigger flat with a garage for Omar's van
Watch local branch closures before deciding on electrics training

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because my job is the thinking kind and it would go first. What would help is a fast-track apprenticeship scheme for adults, with some pay while you train, so people like me can move into trades quickly.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe about the buyers. A family buying their first home already finds it scary. If every update comes from a computer, nobody holds their hand when the chain falls apart.

headlineQuote: A family buying their first home already finds it scary. If every update comes from a computer, nobody holds their hand when the chain falls apart.
portrait: Dana is a **27-year-old sales progressor** at a big national chain, chasing solicitors and brokers all day.
Her role is almost **pure thinking work**, which she sees clearly in every scenario.
She lives with Omar, an **electrician**, and they have over a year's savings.
Her **centre views** show in calm calls for planning and retraining, not blame.
In fast scenarios she'd **join Omar's trade** fitting EV chargers; with ten years, she'd wait for a clear sign.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because her **thinking-heavy** job would go first.
whatWouldHelp: A **paid adult apprenticeship** scheme to move into trades quickly.
